## Independent full proof, clause (ii)

Let V={0,1,2,3,4,5}, with edges between consecutive indices modulo 6. This is finite, loopless and symmetric. Following the cycle connects every pair. Even and odd vertices form a bipartition since every edge changes parity, including 5--0.

For a cycle of length N, two vertices whose forward index separation is a in [0,N] have distance min(a,N-a). The two arcs give upper bounds. A shortest path can be chosen without repeated vertices by deleting a closed subwalk. In a cycle, once its first edge and direction are chosen, a simple path must continue in that direction until reaching the endpoint: taking the other edge would repeat the preceding vertex. Thus it is one of the two arcs, giving the matching lower bound. This argument is a proof, not an automated distance table.

In C6, distances from any vertex to its offsets 1 and 5 are one, to offsets 2 and 4 are two, and to offset 3 are three. Every eccentricity equals three, hence radius=diameter=3>2. For any distinct u,v, square adjacency holds iff they are not opposite. Thus the nonedges are precisely the three unordered pairs {0,3}, {1,4}, {2,5}. The permutation tau interchanges 0 and 3 and fixes the other four vertices. It is its own inverse and preserves the set of opposite pairs. For all pairs, equality is preserved, and for distinct pairs both square adjacency and its failure are preserved. Therefore tau is a square automorphism. The original edge {0,1} maps to {3,1}, of distance two and not an original edge. Thus tau is not an original automorphism, disproving (ii). This witness has r=d and does NOT satisfy clause (i).

Denote nonroot small vertices x1,x2,x3,x4 and large vertices c0,...,c_(2m-1). There are 2m+4 vertices. The construction is finite, simple and connected; every vertex reaches o along a cycle. Removing o separates the two nonroot vertex sets; this cut vertex is allowed. The five-cycle prevents bipartiteness, which is irrelevant to clause (i).

Write b_i=min(i,5-i) and a_j=min(j,2m-j). Within either cycle all distances retain their cycle values. To see the lower bound, a path leaving that cycle must enter the other at o and leave it again at o; deleting that excursion cannot increase its length. A shortest simple path cannot do this. The cycle arcs prove the upper bound. For different nonroot cycles every path must visit o. Its two parts have lengths at least b_i and a_j; conversely shortest cycle arcs concatenate at o. Hence d(x_i,c_j)=b_i+a_j, also valid when j=0. Within C5 the maximum distance is two; within C_(2m) it is m. These statements account for every pair, including the shared root and equal vertices.

For c_j, its large-cycle antipode is at distance m, while x2 (or x3) is at distance a_j+2. Every large-cycle vertex is at distance at most m and every small-cycle vertex at most a_j+2. Consequently every vertex has eccentricity at least m and o attains m, giving radius exactly m. All within-cycle distances are at most m or two; cross distances are at most m+2, attained by x2,c_m. The diameter is exactly m+2. We have r<d, and m+2<=2m-2 iff m>=4. At m=4 the upper bound is equality; for every m>=5 it is strict.
